title: The One With The Baby Shower

jokes.text: Also, your sisters called, neither can make it. What? You mean they're not coming to a social event where there's no men and no booze? That's shocking.
jokes.setup: Monica reports that Rachel's sisters aren't coming to the baby shower
jokes.punchline: Rachel sarcastically notes the event has no men and no booze, implying her sisters are shallow party girls — the sarcasm undercuts any genuine surprise
jokes.explanation: Solid opener — the sarcasm works because it instantly characterizes Rachel's sisters as vapid. The delivery of 'That's shocking' is the engine. Functional but not particularly original.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm shocked. Shocked! My sisters are skipping an event with no men and no alcohol? How is that even possible?

jokes.text: Well, given that we forgot to invite her...it would be an awfully big coincidence if she was.
jokes.setup: Rachel asks in panic whether her mother is going to be at the shower
jokes.punchline: Monica deadpans that since they forgot to invite her, it would be quite the coincidence if she showed up anyway
jokes.explanation: Monica's deadpan logic is well-executed. The understated phrasing 'awfully big coincidence' elevates what could be a straight confession into a funny bit of dry wit. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Will my mom be at the shower?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: About that...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We may have forgotten to invite her.

jokes.text: Well, I don't have a mother. So often I forget other people-- / Oh, give it a rest.
jokes.setup: Phoebe tries to deflect blame for forgetting to invite Rachel's mom by invoking her own motherless upbringing
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately cuts her off with 'Oh, give it a rest,' signaling this is a well-worn excuse
jokes.explanation: This is a great character joke. Phoebe's tragic backstory has been used as a shield before, and Monica's 'give it a rest' implies it's a recurring tactic. The joke works on two levels — it's funny in isolation and funnier if you know the show. High character integration because this is a deeply Phoebe-specific move.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I don't have a mother, so I forget other people have them.

jokes.text: I know. My daughters told me about it...when they received their impromptu invitations a month ago.
jokes.setup: Monica calls Mrs. Green and tries to cover up the mistake by calling the shower 'impromptu'
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Green exposes the lie by noting her daughters got their 'impromptu' invitations a full month ago
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'impromptu' as the weapon of destruction is well-structured. Mrs. Green weaponizes Monica's own cover story against her. Clean, satisfying reversal.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, when I was a kid, my mother used to lock me in the closet...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, we've heard this one. Can you just eat your sandwich?

jokes.text: For not inviting me, or for lying about it? / Oh, my God. My ass is sweating.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Green calmly dismantles Monica's apology by offering two options for what she should be sorry about
jokes.punchline: Monica's stress response is immediately expressed as 'my ass is sweating' — a visceral, undignified physical reaction to being caught
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Mrs. Green's icy composure with Monica's sweaty panic is perfect. 'My ass is sweating' is a genuinely funny, specific, undignified physical detail for the high-strung Monica character. The economy is excellent — it communicates total panic in four words. Memorable line.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Hi Mrs. Green? It's Monica Geller. I'm calling to invite you to... oh my God, what am I doing? You're Rachel's mother. Why am I calling you to invite you to something for Rachel?

jokes.text: Isn't it at 3? / Son of a bitch.
jokes.setup: Monica is relieved to have convinced Mrs. Green to come at 4, the wrong time
jokes.punchline: Phoebe reveals the shower is actually at 3, compounding the disaster Monica just created
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic escalation and economy. Monica barely survives one disaster and immediately tumbles into the next. 'Son of a bitch' as the punchline is blunt and character-perfect for a frustrated Monica. The two-line structure is tight as a drum.

dialogue.speaker: Monica Geller
dialogue.line: It's just an impromptu little shower.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra Green
dialogue.line: Impromptu? Monica, I've had this invitation for a month!

jokes.text: You'll be perfect for this. That's already your name.
jokes.setup: Joey announces that by day he'll be Dr. Drake Ramoray but by night he'll be 'Joey Tribbiani,' said with dramatic flair
jokes.punchline: Chandler flatly notes that 'Joey Tribbiani' is already Joey's real name, deflating the theatrics entirely
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler deadpan. Joey's dramatic self-introduction is punctured instantly. The joke works because it requires the audience to process the gap between Joey's self-seriousness and the obvious reality. High character integration — Chandler is the ideal vehicle for this observation, and Joey's obliviousness is perfectly on-brand. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Mrs. Green, I am so sorry!

dialogue.speaker: Sandra Green
dialogue.line: Oh honey, you're going to have to be more specific. Which thing are you apologizing for?

jokes.text: Okay, I guess we can lose to junior-high girls some other time.
jokes.setup: Joey asks Ross and Chandler to stay and be contestants in his game show practice instead of going to shoot hoops
jokes.punchline: Chandler sarcastically agrees, implying they'd obviously lose at basketball to junior-high girls — self-deprecating but also absurdist
jokes.explanation: Decent throwaway gag. Chandler's self-deprecation is on-brand but the joke doesn't go anywhere particularly surprising. Functional filler humor.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh God, oh God, oh God!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I can explain everything!

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Green
dialogue.line: Can you explain why you told me you were an only child?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That was... that was just a joke!

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Green
dialogue.line: And that you've never been to Long Island?

jokes.text: Ross's overcomplicated self-introduction: 'I'm a paleontologist, I live in New York, I have a son Ben, hi Ben...' / 'I said a little bit, Ross.'
jokes.setup: Joey asks Ross to tell the audience 'a little bit' about himself as game show practice
jokes.punchline: Ross launches into a rambling over-detailed bio; Joey cuts him off with 'I said a little bit, Ross'
jokes.explanation: Ross's inability to be concise and his tendency to over-share is well-characterized. 'Hi, Ben' as an aside to his son during a fake game show audition is a nice touch. Standard sitcom character humor but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Actually, it's at 3.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, crap!

jokes.text: Well, Joey, I'm a headhunter. I hook up out-of-work Soviet scientists with rogue Third World nations. Hi, Rasputin.
jokes.setup: Joey asks Chandler to introduce himself for the game show practice
jokes.punchline: Chandler invents a wildly implausible job description and mirrors Ross's 'Hi Ben' bit with 'Hi, Rasputin'
jokes.explanation: This is a layered joke. The absurd job description ('hook up Soviet scientists with rogue Third World nations') both parodies the game show format and riffs on the long-running joke that nobody knows what Chandler does. 'Hi, Rasputin' perfectly mirrors Ross's 'Hi, Ben' — same structure, exponentially funnier because it's so random. Tight construction.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey Tribbiani is already your name.

jokes.text: What is the capital of Colombia? / Bogoté. / It's Bogoda, but close enough.
jokes.setup: Joey asks a geography question as if hosting a real game show
jokes.punchline: Joey accepts a wrong/garbled answer ('Bogota' mispronounced both ways) with 'close enough,' revealing the game is already poorly designed
jokes.explanation: The joke is that the game show is already broken — a wrong answer is accepted. The mispronunciation layering is a small bonus. Functional setup for the larger Bamboozled absurdist running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We're not going to win. We're going to get crushed by a bunch of junior high girls.

jokes.text: What does a Wicked Wango Card do? / I should know that. [pause] ...A Wicked Wango Card determines whether you go higher or lower. / Higher or lower than what? / This is embarrassing.
jokes.setup: Joey introduces the Wicked Wango Card as a game mechanic
jokes.punchline: Joey has to look it up, then gives an answer that raises more questions than it answers; Ross's follow-up 'higher or lower than what?' exposes the total incoherence of the game
jokes.explanation: The escalating absurdity of the game show rules is well-paced here. Joey having to look up his own game mechanic mid-hosting is a great character beat, and the answer being meaningless is the perfect payoff. 'This is embarrassing' lands as a sincere reaction to the game's nonsense.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Bamboozled!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, come on!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I love this game!

jokes.text: Oh, I told the stripper to be here at 5. That's good, right? / You ordered a stripper for the shower? That is totally inappropriate. / Why? He's gonna be dressed as a baby.
jokes.setup: Phoebe casually mentions she ordered a stripper for the baby shower
jokes.punchline: After Monica's scandalized reaction, Phoebe explains the stripper will be dressed as a baby — which somehow makes it simultaneously worse and funnier
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: (1) inappropriate revelation, (2) justified outrage, (3) a 'defense' that makes it MORE disturbing while being delivered with complete Phoebe innocence. 'He's gonna be dressed as a baby' is a great punchline — it treats the costume as the solution rather than a further complication. Only Phoebe could think this was a reasonable answer. High character integration, great economy, and genuinely quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Come on, introduce yourself for the game show practice.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Chandler Bing. I'm a statistical analysis and data reconfiguration... No wait, that's boring. I'm actually a retired spy. I've infiltrated 47 countries, speak 12 languages, and once saved the world with nothing but a paperclip and my charm.

jokes.text: Oh, hi, Mrs. Green. I'm so glad you could make it. / Try.
jokes.setup: Monica and Phoebe gush over Mrs. Green arriving and apologize profusely, saying they 'could not feel worse about it'
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Green icily responds 'Try.' — a one-word demolition of their apologies
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — one word does enormous work. Mrs. Green's 'Try.' is cold, cutting, and deeply funny precisely because of its brevity. It's the kind of line that gets repeated after viewing. The setup requires Monica's earnest over-apologizing to work, and the contrast is sharp. Elevated by the character: Mrs. Green as imperious WASP matriarch makes this the ideal delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Bogoda!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, it's Bogotá.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's what I said, Bogoda!

jokes.text: She's still mad. / Yeah, I know. / Isn't it great? One less person we have to make small talk with.
jokes.setup: Monica observes that Mrs. Green is still angry at them
jokes.punchline: Phoebe reframes Mrs. Green's silent treatment as a social benefit — fewer small-talk obligations
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's ability to find the silver lining in social catastrophe is well-used here. The reframing is her character's coping mechanism. Functional and character-specific but not particularly sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: The Wicked Wango Card determines if you go higher or lower.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What's a Wicked Wango Card?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: ...I don't know.

jokes.text: Okay. I can do that. Heh. / I gotta go powder my ass.
jokes.setup: Monica has just resolved to be okay with Mrs. Green being mad at her
jokes.punchline: She immediately leaves to 'powder her ass,' revisiting the stress-sweating joke from earlier
jokes.explanation: The callback to the ass-sweating joke works as a running gag. It reinforces Monica's anxiety is still active despite her forced resolution, and 'powder my ass' is a funny, specific phrase. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, settle down everyone. I am the host of this game show and I will be asking the questions.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey, you don't even know what the game is.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That doesn't matter! I have the card, I have the suit, and I have this very authoritative voice.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You sound like you're selling paper towels.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I do NOT! And for that comment, you lose a turn.

jokes.text: Now, have you picked your nanny yet? I don't want you to just use your housekeeper because it'll just split her focus. / Oh. Actually, I'm not gonna use a nanny. And I don't even have a housekeeper. / It's like you're a cave person.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Green assumes Rachel has the same upper-class lifestyle she raised her in
jokes.punchline: Rachel reveals she has neither a nanny nor a housekeeper; Mrs. Green responds as if this is primitive — 'It's like you're a cave person'
jokes.explanation: Mrs. Green's oblivious class snobbery is well-played. 'It's like you're a cave person' is an absurd overreaction that lands because it's so specific to Sandra's character. Good character integration for both Rachel's independence arc and Mrs. Green's out-of-touch privilege.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ordering a stripper for the shower is inappropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What if she wore a baby costume?

jokes.text: Mrs. K taught me Spanish. I actually think I remember some of it: [speaks Spanish badly]
jokes.setup: Rachel fondly remembers Mrs. K the nanny who taught her Spanish
jokes.punchline: She demonstrates her Spanish and it's clearly garbled/terrible — the nostalgic claim doesn't hold up to demonstration
jokes.explanation: A predictable but functional gag — the character boasts about a skill they clearly don't have. Works because Jennifer Aniston's physical performance likely elevates it, but as written it's fairly stock.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We feel terrible about forgetting to invite you.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, we couldn't feel worse.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra Green
dialogue.line: Wanna bet?

jokes.text: Oh, Rachel. / What? / I just had the greatest idea. I'm gonna come live with you.
jokes.setup: Rachel has just said she can't afford full-time help
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Green announces she will simply move in herself — framing an imposition as a generous gift
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom complication reveal — the solution becomes the new problem. Well-timed and character-consistent for Mrs. Green's oblivious benevolence. The 'greatest idea' framing contrasts nicely with Rachel's horror.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Sandra is still mad at us.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, that's good! Now we don't have to invite her to stuff!

jokes.text: Aw, look at you. You have tears in your eyes. [pause] Yes, yes, I do.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Green interprets Rachel's tears of horror as tears of joy at the news
jokes.punchline: Rachel's flat 'Yes, yes, I do' — a deadpan confirmation that lets the audience fill in what kind of tears they really are
jokes.explanation: The gap between what Mrs. Green thinks is happening and what Rachel is experiencing is the engine. Rachel's flat agreement is a great piece of controlled delivery — she can't even muster a lie. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm just going to go powder my ass.

jokes.text: The Wheel has not been my friend tonight, Joey.
jokes.setup: Joey asks Ross if he wants to spin the Wheel of Mayhem
jokes.punchline: Ross has fully bought into the nonsense game and refers to the Wheel with genuine personal grievance, as if it has a personality
jokes.explanation: Ross's total commitment to the fake game is a consistent source of comedy in this sequence. The line is funny because it confirms the men have completely surrendered to the absurd premise. Good character integration — Ross takes everything too seriously.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra Green
dialogue.line: You look like a cheerleader in trouble.

jokes.text: No, dude, you gotta hold your breath till you're ready to answer the question. It's part of the game.
jokes.setup: Joey tells Ross to 'hold his breath' before a question; Chandler protests that Ross won't actually hold his breath
jokes.punchline: Joey defends the arbitrary rule earnestly as if it's a legitimate game mechanic
jokes.explanation: Joey's earnest defense of increasingly absurd rules is part of the episode's sustained Bamboozled bit. Consistent and functional but not a standout within the sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I won't use a nanny or housekeeper.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra Green
dialogue.line: Oh honey, that's like living in the Dark Ages. You might as well be churning butter and carrying water from a well.

jokes.text: Triskaidekaphobia. / Fear of Triscuits. / No. No. Fear of the number 13. / Fear of Triscuits? / It's possible. They have really sharp edges.
jokes.setup: Joey struggles to pronounce 'triskaidekaphobia' and reads it as a possible fear of Triscuits (the cracker)
jokes.punchline: After Joey correctly identifies it as fear of 13, Ross circles back to genuinely defend the Triscuit theory — 'they have really sharp edges'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The wordplay (triskaideKAPHOBIA / TRIScuit) is legitimate and not forced. The structure is excellent: Joey mishears, correction is given, then Ross unexpectedly resurrects the wrong answer with a deadpan physical justification. The beat where it seems resolved and then Ross genuinely considers whether Triscuit-fear is valid is the comedic peak. 'They have really sharp edges' is legitimately quotable and character-perfect for Ross's compulsive need to analyze things.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Mrs. K taught me Spanish.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: ¿Cómo estás?

jokes.text: Wait a minute. I believe I'm entitled to use my Angel Pass for a free turn. / This game makes no sense. / You're just upset because you're losing.
jokes.setup: Chandler invokes a game mechanic called the 'Angel Pass'
jokes.punchline: Ross protests the game makes no sense; Chandler retorts he's just upset because he's losing — implying Chandler himself has accepted the nonsense game
jokes.explanation: Good running escalation of the absurd game. The reversal — Chandler was complaining moments ago but now defends the game because he's winning — is a nice character beat. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I can't afford full-time help.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra Green
dialogue.line: Well, I'm free. I could help you out.

jokes.text: Oh, come on, Ross. I think we're all losers here.
jokes.setup: Chandler tells Ross he's just upset because he's losing Bamboozled
jokes.punchline: Joey, the game show host, earnestly assures them they're all losers — accidentally honest about the situation
jokes.explanation: Joey's accidental honesty is a good character beat. He means it as an encouraging game-show host line but it lands as genuine self-awareness the character doesn't intend. The economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra Green
dialogue.line: Oh honey, are you crying? Happy tears?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yes... tears. From joy.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra Green
dialogue.line: That's wonderful!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, actually, these are terror tears.

jokes.text: You must choose, Mr. Bing. / Either. It makes no difference. / Choose, you jackass.
jokes.setup: Joey maintains the professional game-show-host persona while Chandler refuses to engage with the meaningless choice
jokes.punchline: Joey breaks character entirely: 'Choose, you jackass'
jokes.explanation: The snap from 'Mr. Bing' formal address to 'you jackass' is a perfect tonal gear-shift. It's funny because Joey has been so earnest about the game and Chandler's indifference finally breaks him. The contrast between the professional framing and the insult is well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay. Now hold your breath.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? Why?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Because those are the rules.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What rules? You just made that up!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, now it's a rule.

jokes.text: Okay, you picked the Gimme Card. You get all of Ross' points. / What? / This game is kind of fun.
jokes.setup: Chandler reluctantly picks a card; Joey reveals it gives him all of Ross's points
jokes.punchline: Chandler, who was complaining about the game moments ago, immediately declares 'This game is kind of fun' now that he's winning
jokes.explanation: Classic hypocrisy reversal — Chandler's immediate conversion upon gaining an advantage is a solid character beat. The speed of the reversal is what makes it funny. Good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's ridiculous. Holding your breath doesn't work.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What are you talking about? Of course it works! When you hold your breath, the other person can't—

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Proving my point.

jokes.text: Why did you invite my mother? / She wants to move in with me and Ross to help take care of the baby. / For how long? / Eight weeks. / I mean, I love my mother, but, my God, a long lunch with her is taxing.
jokes.setup: Rachel reveals Mrs. Green wants to move in for eight weeks
jokes.punchline: Rachel admits she loves her mother but a 'long lunch with her is taxing' — immediately undercutting her professed love
jokes.explanation: The 'I love X, but...' structure followed immediately by the undermining qualifier is a standard sitcom pattern. Executed competently and the 'long lunch is taxing' is specific enough to be funny.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What's triskaidekaphobia?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, that's when you're afraid of Triscuits.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, it's the fear of the number thirteen.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Right, right, Triscuits. I know what I said.

jokes.text: I personally would be honored if she wanted to live with me. / She can't hear you.
jokes.setup: Phoebe loudly announces she'd be honored to have Mrs. Green live with her
jokes.punchline: Monica flatly points out that Mrs. Green can't hear Phoebe's grandstanding from across the room — it's purely performative
jokes.explanation: Monica's precision deflation of Phoebe's posturing is well-timed. 'She can't hear you' is the ideal four-word response — it acknowledges the performance for what it is. Good economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, no, it makes perfect sense! 'Trisca' — fear of, 'uits' — Triscuits. It's a perfectly valid phobia!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Ross, that's not how words work.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, and I suppose you have a better explanation?

jokes.text: This is great. Now she's gonna be mad at Rachel. And I'm just gonna swoop in there and be like the daughter she never had.
jokes.setup: Monica has told Rachel to go tell her mother she doesn't want her to move in
jokes.punchline: Phoebe reveals her scheme to 'swoop in' and become the favored surrogate daughter once Rachel falls from grace
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's self-serving scheme is delivered with her characteristic unapologetic honesty. The 'daughter she never had' line lands because Mrs. Green literally has daughters — it's delightfully oblivious.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Chandler is upset because he's losing.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Everyone is losing by playing this terrible game.

jokes.text: I have new respect for Chandler.
jokes.setup: During Bamboozled, Chandler wins all of Ross's points via the Gimme Card
jokes.punchline: Ross's quiet admission of newfound respect for Chandler, apparently because Chandler now has his points
jokes.explanation: A quiet throwaway that gets a mild chuckle. Ross's reasoning is absurd but the joke isn't developed enough to be more than a minor beat.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't care which one we pick, they're both fine.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, you've said that like five times! Just pick one!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I literally don't care.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Chandler, you're the most indecisive person I've ever met! How do you even get dressed in the morning?

jokes.text: Yes, and I think that the first gift that Rachel opens should be from the grandmother of the baby. Because you're the most important person in this room. And in the world.
jokes.setup: It's time to open presents; Phoebe nominates Mrs. Green's gift first
jokes.punchline: Phoebe escalates from 'most important person in this room' to 'in the world' — nakedly transparent flattery in pursuit of her scheme
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'room' to 'world' is a nice comic beat — Phoebe can't even maintain plausible flattery. The callback to her scheming makes it funnier in context.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You know what? I'm actually really good at this game. I like this game now.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh come on, Chandler, you can't just start liking it because you're winning.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No points for you!

jokes.text: Well, um, I don't have a gift because I wasn't invited until the last minute. But thank you so much, dear, for bringing that to everybody's attention.
jokes.setup: Phoebe volunteers Mrs. Green's gift first, unaware she doesn't have one
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Green exposes her lack of a gift and thanks Phoebe with dripping sarcasm for making it public
jokes.explanation: Mrs. Green's icy 'thank you so much for bringing that to everybody's attention' is a great line — she turns her own embarrassment into a weapon against Phoebe. The payoff of Phoebe's sycophantic scheme backfiring immediately is satisfying structurally.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: She can't hear you. She's in the other room.

jokes.text: Well, I kind of did. / What? / Me. Eight weeks of me.
jokes.setup: Rachel graciously tells her mother it's okay she didn't bring a gift
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Green says she did bring a gift — herself, for eight weeks — with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: 'Me. Eight weeks of me.' is a beautifully economical line — the pause before 'Eight weeks of me' and the self-satisfied delivery make it. Mrs. Green's complete obliviousness to how this lands is the core of her character comedy in this episode.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, you want to sleep on the couch?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, what if you want to sleep in my bed?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What if you want to sleep in my bed with me?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, what if you never leave?

jokes.text: Remember Twinkles? / He was a hamster. I'm not gonna vacuum up my baby.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Green raises doubts about Rachel's parenting ability and says 'remember Twinkles?'
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately knows this is about a dead hamster and defensively says she won't vacuum up her baby
jokes.explanation: The joke does a lot with very little. We never hear the Twinkles story but we immediately understand it, and Rachel's preemptive defense — 'I'm not gonna vacuum up my baby' — implies the story is bad enough that this is the first comparison she thinks of. Dark, specific, and character-perfect. 'I'm not gonna vacuum up my baby' is a genuinely funny line.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You should tell your mother you don't need her help. You need to be independent.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Really? I thought you liked my mom.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I do! But... okay, fine. If she's not around helping you all the time, maybe she'll have more time to help me. And then I'll be her favorite.

jokes.text: Wait a minute. That can't be right. Is that a beer bong for a baby?
jokes.setup: Rachel opens a baby shower gift and examines a breast pump
jokes.punchline: She identifies it as 'a beer bong for a baby' — a hilariously wrong but logically coherent misidentification
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's better jokes. 'Beer bong for a baby' is a funny, specific, and structurally interesting misidentification — it's wrong in a way that makes internal sense (a tube for delivering liquid to a small person). The visual of Rachel genuinely puzzling over this is strong. The 'Did I say I was done guessing?' follow-up adds another layer. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Monica, you are SO manipulative! You're like Chandler when he plays mind games!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I am not!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yes, you are! You totally just pulled a Chandler Bing on us!

jokes.text: Darling, that's a breast pump. / Heh. Did I say I was done guessing? Okay, thank you for that.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Green corrects Rachel's 'beer bong for a baby' misidentification
jokes.punchline: Rachel's mock-defensive 'Did I say I was done guessing?' — trying to maintain dignity while being obviously clueless
jokes.explanation: The 'did I say I was done guessing' line is a good piece of face-saving comedy. Rachel's flustered damage control is character-consistent. The direct follow-on from #36 extends the laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You're the most important person here, so you should open the first gift.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra Green
dialogue.line: Oh, well thank you for pointing out that I've been excluded from everything else.

jokes.text: Oh, wow. What's this? / It's a Diaper Genie. / Oh, it dispenses clean diapers. / No, it's where you put dirty ones. / Well, that's gross. Why don't you just take it outside and throw it in a Dumpster?
jokes.setup: Rachel receives a Diaper Genie and assumes it dispenses clean diapers
jokes.punchline: Corrected that it's for dirty diapers, Rachel proposes just throwing dirty diapers in a dumpster instead
jokes.explanation: Rachel's cluelessness about baby products is the comedic engine of this whole sequence. The Dumpster suggestion is a good specific detail that shows how unprepared she is. Standard but well-executed setup-punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You're the most important person.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra Green
dialogue.line: Oh, so everyone else is less important?

jokes.text: You're gonna do that 10 times a day? / What, it goes 10 times a day? / What are we feeding this baby, Indian food?
jokes.setup: Monica points out that taking diapers to a dumpster would happen 10 times a day
jokes.punchline: Rachel's shock at the frequency leads her to ask 'what are we feeding this baby, Indian food?' — using the stereotype for digestive potency as a comedic frame
jokes.explanation: The punchline relies on a lazy ethnic stereotype (Indian food = gastrointestinal distress) which makes it feel somewhat dated and cheap. The setup escalation is good but the punchline falls back on a cliché. Below average for the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I can totally handle a baby. Babies are completely different from hamsters.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra Green
dialogue.line: Really? Because I seem to recall a certain incident with 'Twinkles.'

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: That was an accident! I didn't see him in the pile of laundry. How was I supposed to know he was in there before I turned on the vacuum?

dialogue.speaker: Sandra Green
dialogue.line: Exactly my point.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: But a baby won't fit in the vacuum, so...

jokes.text: I don't know, I'd leave it on the changing table? / [ALL GASP]
jokes.setup: Someone asks what Rachel would do with the baby while she takes diapers to the trash
jokes.punchline: Rachel's answer — leave it on the changing table — triggers a collective gasp from the entire party
jokes.explanation: The collective gasp is a good multi-camera moment — the horror of the entire room reacting simultaneously heightens Rachel's obliviousness. The rising stakes of the gift-opening sequence make this land well.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What is this? A beer bong?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's a breast pump, Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I was about to say, that seems like a lot of work for a beer.

jokes.text: Of course, I know that. I mean, of course you never leave a baby alone. Ha, ha. I mean, it would-- She wouldn't be safe. You know, not as safe as she would be with me, the baby dummy.
jokes.setup: Rachel has just been gasped at for suggesting leaving a baby on a changing table
jokes.punchline: Rachel's increasingly desperate attempt to walk it back ends with 'with me, the baby dummy' — a self-aware admission of total incompetence while still trying to save face
jokes.explanation: Rachel's spiral of back-pedaling is well-performed territory. 'The baby dummy' as a self-description is a good button for the cringe sequence. The humor is in watching her dig the hole deeper.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, a breast pump! Of course! I knew that. I was just... testing you.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know, to make sure you knew what it was. Because that's the kind of friend I am.

jokes.text: Okay, you know what? Opening the presents is a little overwhelming right now. So I think I'm just gonna maybe open them all a little bit later. But thank you all for coming, and for these beautiful gifts, and this basket is beautiful. / It's actually a bassinet.
jokes.setup: Rachel wraps up present-opening early to escape her embarrassment and thanks everyone for 'this beautiful basket'
jokes.punchline: Monica quietly corrects her — it's a bassinet, not a basket — one final proof of Rachel's ignorance as she tries to exit gracefully
jokes.explanation: Perfect button for the gift-opening sequence. Rachel thinks she's finally ending the disaster gracefully, but Monica's gentle correction shows she can't even name the items correctly as she thanks people. The timing and economy are excellent — Monica's correction is the ideal understated punctuation.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, so it just... keeps them in there? All of them?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's airtight, so you don't smell them.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Why would you do that? Why wouldn't you just throw them in a dumpster?

jokes.text: Okay, Mommy, don't ever leave me.
jokes.setup: Rachel has just failed spectacularly at demonstrating any baby knowledge and been trying to push her mother away
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately reverses her position and clings to her mother
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic reversal. Rachel was trying to be independent and ended by clinging to her mom. The economy is excellent — five words close out the whole sequence. The '...Okay, Mommy, don't ever leave me' as a beat on the end of the disastrous gift-opening works as both joke and character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You're going to throw the baby in the dumpster?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? No! The diapers!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I had no idea you had to change them that often!

jokes.text: In what John Huston film would you hear this line: 'Badges? We don't need no stinking badges.' / Treasure of the Sierra Madre. / Correct. There's a possible Backwards Bonus. / Madre Sierra the of Treasure. / Yes.
jokes.setup: Joey gives a legitimate trivia question which Ross answers correctly
jokes.punchline: Joey introduces a 'Backwards Bonus' — saying the answer backwards — and Ross earnestly does it, and Joey accepts it
jokes.explanation: The Backwards Bonus is an inspired piece of absurdist game show design. That Ross knows the actual answer and then earnestly says it backwards, and Joey accepts it without question, is a great beat. The increasingly elaborate Bamboozled mechanics continue to escalate amusingly.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ten diapers a day? That's so many! I thought babies only went to the bathroom like, twice a day.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, it's ten times a day. Babies have very fast metabolisms.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Well, that must be because of all the spicy food they eat.

jokes.text: I'd like a Wicked Wango Card. / Okay. It's an audio question. Name this television theme song: [humming I Dream of Jeannie] / Oh, my God. Okay, I know this. Give me a second. / Tell it to the Time Turtle. / Shut up.
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to identify an audio clue under time pressure
jokes.punchline: Joey introduces a 'Time Turtle' — yet another arbitrary game mechanic — and Chandler's 'Shut up' is a contestant breaking the fourth wall of the game
jokes.explanation: The 'Time Turtle' is another great absurdist game element — the escalation of ridiculous Bamboozled mechanics is consistent and funny. Chandler's 'Shut up' is a good release valve. The humor is sustained well across the whole Bamboozled sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I could leave her in the car.

dialogue.speaker: Everyone
dialogue.line: *horrified gasps*

jokes.text: Super Speedy Speed Round. / Is there a Hopping Bonus? / Of course.
jokes.setup: The wheel lands on a Super Speedy Speed Round
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately asks if there's a 'Hopping Bonus' — he has become so fluent in Bamboozled that he now knows additional sub-mechanics; Joey confirms it as if it's obvious
jokes.explanation: Ross asking about the Hopping Bonus confirms how completely both men have been absorbed by the game. 'Of course' from Joey treats this as obvious, further deepening the absurdist world-building. The escalation of commitment is the ongoing joke.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? No, no, no! I didn't mean leave the baby alone alone. I just meant like, you know, give the baby some space to, like, develop its own personality.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I'm such a baby dummy.

jokes.text: But you forgot to switch legs between questions. So no Hopping Bonus. / Oh! Every time.
jokes.setup: Ross correctly answers multiple speed round questions
jokes.punchline: Joey disqualifies the Hopping Bonus because Ross didn't switch hopping legs between questions; Ross's 'every time' implies this has happened before — in a game they invented hours ago
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a highlight of the Bamboozled sequence. The rule itself (alternating legs) is absurd enough, but Ross's 'Every time' implies he has repeatedly made this same error in a game that was invented TODAY. The implication that they've played enough to have recurring mistakes is brilliantly absurd. This is the peak of the Bamboozled escalation — the joke has perfect structure, is character-integrated (Ross's competitive nature), and the 'every time' is an instantly quotable line. Comparable to quality anchor examples.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, that's a bassinet.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I knew that. I was just... testing you.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Mom? MOM?! I need you!

jokes.text: Oh, my God. Congratulations, Ross. Because, Chandler, you've been Bamboozled. / No! / Yes! / This is the best game ever!
jokes.setup: Joey dramatically announces the game's conclusion
jokes.punchline: Chandler, who was mocking the game throughout, shouts 'No!' with genuine anguish; Ross declares 'This is the best game ever!' having also been a skeptic
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff for the Bamboozled running gag. Both Ross and Chandler began as reluctant skeptics and both are now fully consumed — Chandler devastated, Ross elated. The irony that the two people who mocked it are most emotionally invested is the ideal comedic payoff. 'This is the best game ever!' from Ross, who was refusing to hold his breath an hour ago, is excellent character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Ooh ooh ooh! Eee eee eee!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, he's doing 'Hungry Monkey' again.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, we know.

jokes.text: Why are you all red and sweaty? / I just Bamboozled Chandler. / Which is not a sexual thing.
jokes.setup: Phoebe sees Ross flushed and sweaty and asks why
jokes.punchline: Ross explains he Bamboozled Chandler, then immediately adds 'which is not a sexual thing' — anticipating a misreading that wasn't yet there
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure — the setup (red and sweaty from game exertion) triggers the double entendre potential, and Ross's preemptive disclaimer 'which is not a sexual thing' is funnier than any actual sexual misinterpretation would have been. The joke works because Ross says the quiet part loud before anyone else does. Very quotable and the kind of joke that earns a rewatch.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, you got all the answers right? That's amazing!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know, right? I'm on a roll!

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.line: Congratulations! You've won the bonus round! Now, for an extra $10,000, you must switch legs and answer one more question.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Switch legs? But I'm on this leg!

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.line: Those are the rules. Switch legs or forfeit the bonus.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: This always happens to me! Why do they always make me switch legs?!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Just switch, man. Come on!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Fine, fine... *switches legs* See? Now I'm gonna lose.

jokes.text: Well, that was a quick shower. / Not if you were here.
jokes.setup: Ross comments that the baby shower was quick
jokes.punchline: Monica's dry 'Not if you were here' — implying the shower was anything but quick from her point of view
jokes.explanation: Clean, economic line. Monica's perspective — having managed the disaster of the shower — is crystallized perfectly. The gap between Ross's breezy observation and Monica's experience is well-played.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm picking a card. This is it. This is my card.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Alright, you got 'Bamboozled.'

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? No, no, no! That's not... I lose everything?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, man, those are the rules.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, this is the worst day of my life. I'm done. I'm moving to Yemen.

jokes.text: We did. But my mom got us the greatest gift of all. / A Play-Doh Barbershop? / No. She's going to live with us for eight weeks.
jokes.setup: Rachel tells Ross her mom got them the greatest gift of all
jokes.punchline: Ross guesses 'A Play-Doh Barbershop?' — a hilariously specific, random, and wrong guess — before Rachel delivers the actually terrible news
jokes.explanation: 'Play-Doh Barbershop' is a brilliantly specific wrong guess. The randomness is exactly right — it's the kind of non-sequitur that shows genuine comedic writing instinct. The structure works because the actual answer (Mrs. Green moving in) is worse than any guess, which makes Ross's reaction funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't know anything about babies! What if I do something wrong?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh God, I think I'm gonna be sick. Where's the diaper pail?

jokes.text: You're not serious. I mean, she's a very nice woman, but there's no way we can take eight weeks of her. She'll drive us totally crazy-- / Hi, Ross. / Hey, roomie.
jokes.setup: Ross is mid-rant about how Mrs. Green will drive them crazy
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Green appears behind him mid-sentence; his instant pivot to 'Hey, roomie' is the comedic landing
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom 'caught talking about someone who appears behind you' gag — but Ross's pivot to 'Hey, roomie' is a great specific choice. The word 'roomie' in Ross's panicked voice sells it entirely. The structure is traditional but the execution is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I was playing basketball, okay? I got all sweaty from playing basketball.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, you were playing with balls?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yes, Phoebe, basketballs. It's a game. You bounce the ball, you throw it in the hoop.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, okay.

jokes.text: It's a pleasure to meet you, Ray. [in embellished voice]
jokes.setup: Joey meets the actual producer of Bamboozled
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately slips into his exaggerated TV host voice for a simple introduction
jokes.explanation: Joey staying in character even for a mundane introduction is a consistent character beat. Functional but not a standout gag.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That shower ended pretty quickly.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, well it felt like forever in there.

jokes.text: Joey, didn't your agents give you the revised rules? We've eliminated all that. No wheel. No cards. / What? Why? / Well, the game was too complicated and research showed people didn't follow it.
jokes.setup: Joey begins hosting the actual audition using all the elaborate Bamboozled mechanics he's been practicing
jokes.punchline: The producer reveals all the fun mechanics have been eliminated because they were 'too complicated'
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural payoff. The entire Bamboozled subplot — with all its lovingly absurd mechanics — exists so that this moment can land: everything they practiced is gone. The audience has been absorbing these rules right alongside Joey, so the elimination hits the same way it hits him. Great sitcom plotting.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: My mom got us the greatest gift.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: A new coffee table!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh wow, that's nice.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, that's not it. My mom is moving in with us.

jokes.text: What's complicated? You spin the Wheel of Mayhem to go up the Ladder of Chance, past the Mud Hut through the Rainbow Ring to get to the Golden Monkey. You yank his tail, and boom, you're in Paradise Pond. / Yeah. All that's gone.
jokes.setup: Joey defends the game mechanics after being told they've been cut
jokes.punchline: Joey recites the entire game path from memory in a rush, making it sound even more insane — 'yank his tail, boom, Paradise Pond' — only to be told 'all that's gone'
jokes.explanation: Joey's passionate recitation of the full game path is a comedic highlight. The list itself is funny (Mud Hut, Rainbow Ring, Golden Monkey, Paradise Pond), delivered with Joey's earnest enthusiasm as if this is perfectly reasonable. The blunt 'all that's gone' deflates it perfectly. The character integration is excellent — Joey has memorized a meaningless thing with the fervor he never applies to anything practical.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Mom's moving in with us.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? When?

dialogue.speaker: Sandra Green
dialogue.line: Hello, roomie!

jokes.text: Well, what's fun about that? You expect me to be the host of a boring game that's just people standing around answering questions? / Well, there'll be women in bikinis holding up the scores. / [immediately in embellished voice] Let's play Bamboozled.
jokes.setup: Joey is horrified at the stripped-down version of the game
jokes.punchline: The producer adds there will be women in bikinis; Joey instantly switches back to full enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Perfect Joey character comedy. His 'principles' about game design dissolve the instant women in bikinis are mentioned, and he snaps back to his host persona without missing a beat. The character integration is excellent — this is quintessentially Joey, and the speed of the reversal is what makes it funny.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, how's it going? I'm Joey Tribbiani.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm an actor. I've been in a lot of TV shows and movies. You might have seen me.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Ah, well, actually, I prefer the finer things in life. I'm quite the thespian, you know. My craft is very important to me, and I take my work very seriously indeed.

jokes.text: And all those dinosaur knickknacks you have, Ross, I thought they might be more at home in the garage. / Well, we don't have a garage. / Did I say garage? I meant garbage.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Green has just moved in and immediately starts rearranging the apartment by suggesting Ross's dinosaur items go to the 'garage'
jokes.punchline: When corrected that there's no garage, she smoothly says 'Did I say garage? I meant garbage' — a barely-disguised attack delivered with patrician smoothness
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The 'garage/garbage' slip-and-recover is brilliantly constructed — Mrs. Green's thin veneer of politeness peels back to reveal casual hostility. The delivery implication ('Did I say garage?') of feigned confusion before the reveal is perfect. The line is memorable, quotable, and completely character-specific to Sandra Green's imperious nature. The economy is exceptional — the entire joke is nine words.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Too complicated? It's simple! You roll the dice, move your piece around the board, collect cards, build your empire, fight off the dragon, solve the riddle, find the hidden treasure, and whoever reaches Shangri-La first wins!

jokes.text: That's true. You do have another child. / Yeah. / With another woman. / Have you no control, Ross?
jokes.setup: Ross is making the case for his competence as a father by citing his son Ben
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Green's pointed 'With another woman. Have you no control, Ross?' — turning Ross's credential into an indictment of his personal life
jokes.explanation: Mrs. Green's takedown of Ross via his own evidence is sharp. 'Have you no control, Ross?' is a great character line — the patrician judgmentalism applied to a situation that isn't really about control at all. It's also an absurdly old-fashioned formulation ('Have you no control') which suits Mrs. Green perfectly. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A question-answer game? That's boring. That's what all game shows are!

jokes.text: Well, then you don't need me to live with you. / Yes! / Yes. You're gonna be so missed.
jokes.setup: Ross successfully convinces Mrs. Green he can handle the baby, so she agrees she doesn't need to stay
jokes.punchline: Ross says 'Yes!' with undisguised triumph; Phoebe immediately covers with 'Yes. You're gonna be so missed.' — transparently fake
jokes.explanation: Ross's involuntary 'Yes!' is a good beat and Phoebe's instant cover is well-timed. The transparency of Phoebe's 'you're gonna be so missed' makes it funnier. Standard sitcom timing but executed well.

dialogue.speaker: Producer
dialogue.line: Hey, look on the bright side. We can get you bikini-clad women to jump around on stage.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Really? When do we start?

jokes.text: Hello? I still don't know what the hell I'm doing.
jokes.setup: Everyone has been solving the problem of Mrs. Green moving in; Rachel's fears about being a good mother have been sidelined
jokes.punchline: Rachel re-inserts herself into the conversation to point out her original problem hasn't been solved
jokes.explanation: A good beat that reconnects the episode's emotional core with the comedy. The 'Hello?' is a funny way to re-enter. Functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra Green
dialogue.line: All this dinosaur stuff should go in the garage.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra Green
dialogue.line: I mean, the garbage.

jokes.text: When you first came to the city, you were this spoiled, helpless little girl who still used Daddy's credit cards, remember? / I hope you're going somewhere with this.
jokes.setup: Ross is building toward an inspiring speech about Rachel's growth
jokes.punchline: Rachel's nervous 'I hope you're going somewhere with this' — she can hear how bad the setup sounds and isn't sure Ross will stick the landing
jokes.explanation: Rachel's pre-emptive concern is well-delivered. It's funny because she's right — the setup sounds like an insult — and her worried intervention makes the audience share her anxiety. Good character integration and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I have a son with Carol.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Green
dialogue.line: A son? Ross, how many women are you with?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, Carol is my ex-wife. We had a son together before we got divorced.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Green
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, that's still one too many.

jokes.text: It's like I'm not here. Which I almost wasn't.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Green is leaving and says she'll let herself out
jokes.punchline: She adds 'which I almost wasn't' — a final passive-aggressive reminder of the forgotten invitation, delivered in a breezily self-satisfied tone
jokes.explanation: Mrs. Green gets a final passive-aggressive parting shot that callbacks to the episode's opening disaster. The lightness of the delivery ('it's like I'm not here — which I almost wasn't') while being clearly pointed is excellent character writing. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm still here, and I still have no idea what's going on.

jokes.text: It's like I'm not here. Which I almost wasn't.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Green is saying goodbye and trying to exit gracefully.
jokes.punchline: Her parting shot — 'It's like I'm not here. Which I almost wasn't' — is a last passive-aggressive reminder of the invitation snub, delivered with a smile as she leaves.
jokes.explanation: Sandra Green's farewell passive-aggression is perfectly in character. The structure — 'It's like I'm not here' (literal, fine) → 'Which I almost wasn't' (the sting) — is elegant. She lands one last punch while pretending not to, which is very much her style.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What should I do about Mrs. Green being mad at me?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, you shouldn't feel guilty. She's been mean to you for years. Remember when she said your shower curtain was nice, but then asked if you got it at a yard sale?

jokes.text: [Rachel laughs nervously] You're just so funny. You're so funny. What do I do?
jokes.setup: Mrs. Green makes her passive-aggressive parting comment and walks away while Monica and Rachel are stuck watching
jokes.punchline: Rachel's helpless 'What do I do?' — she is simultaneously charmed and victimized and has no idea how to respond
jokes.explanation: A good reaction beat that captures Rachel's helplessness, but it's more a character moment than a joke. The laughter followed by 'What do I do?' is relatable but not particularly crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know what, young lady—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, no, old lady—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Lady.

jokes.text: Yeah, I mean, if you wanna say anything to her, I'd tell her off. / Really? / Uh-huh.
jokes.setup: Monica has just finished a pep talk about how Rachel doesn't need to do anything about Mrs. Green's rudeness
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately pivots to telling Rachel to 'tell her off' — the pep talk ends with Monica encouraging a confrontation
jokes.explanation: Monica's rapid reversal — from 'you don't have to do anything' to 'tell her off' — reveals her own unresolved frustration with Mrs. Green. Character-specific and well-paced within the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Monica, just end it! End it now before it gets worse!

jokes.text: Maybe it's time you took a good, hard look in the mirror, young lady. / Old lady. / Lady.
jokes.setup: Monica has confronted Mrs. Green and is in full righteous mode, using the phrase 'young lady'
jokes.punchline: Monica catches herself and self-corrects to 'old lady,' then Rachel frantically signals to just say 'lady' — the two of them doing rapid damage control mid-confrontation
jokes.explanation: The three-beat correction ('young lady / old lady / lady') is sharp physical-verbal comedy — the kind of rapid negotiation between two people mid-speech that feels spontaneous. The escalation from correction to compromise is well-structured. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Mrs. Green, I need to talk to you about what happened at Thanksgiving.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I can't believe you said those things about me in front of everyone!

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Green
dialogue.line: Monica, I was just being honest.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Honest?! You called me a control freak who can't let anyone else cook in her kitchen!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I can't... I can't feel my legs... Why can't I feel my legs?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Is anyone else hot? I'm sweating. I'm shaking. What is happening to me?

jokes.text: Wrap it up. Wrap it up. Wrap it up.
jokes.setup: Monica is mid-confrontation with Mrs. Green and seems to be going off-script
jokes.punchline: Rachel urgently signals Monica to wrap it up, as if stage-managing a performance that's running long
jokes.explanation: A good visual beat — Rachel frantically flagging Monica down like a floor producer. Works as a physical comedy inference and character dynamic between the two friends.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Mrs. Green, I'm so sorry about what happened at Thanksgiving. I feel terrible and I just want to—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: [falls/runs into something]

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: —apologize. As I was saying, I'm really, really sorry.

jokes.text: So whenever you're ready to apologize to me, I will forgive you. Good day.
jokes.setup: Monica has just confronted Mrs. Green with great conviction
jokes.punchline: She closes with 'Good day' — an absurdly formal and theatrical exit line that's too stagey to land naturally
jokes.explanation: 'Good day' as a sitcom exit line is fairly stock, but Monica's earnestness about it is character-appropriate. It lands as a mild laugh — the theatricality of the confrontation peaking in an overcooked exit.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay Rachel, this is the baby knowledge round. Question one: What do you do if your baby won't stop crying?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Um... sing to them?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, that's incorrect. You're eliminated from motherhood.

jokes.text: I can't feel my legs.
jokes.setup: Monica has just finished her confrontation speech and walked away from Mrs. Green.
jokes.punchline: The adrenaline crash: Monica's 'I can't feel my legs' communicates pure post-confrontation shock — the physical comedy of her body shutting down after the stress.
jokes.explanation: Good physical comedy beat. Monica's body physically shutting down after the confrontation is funny and character-true — she desperately wanted to do that but it terrified her. 'I can't feel my legs' is concise and gets a solid laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel Green, you are a terrible mother!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, what? That's not even a real thing. This is ridiculous.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You can't just declare someone a terrible mother based on a game show format!

jokes.text: Mrs. Green? Okay, I'm really sorry. I apologize. If you just-- Aah! [THUDDING] / Okay. I bit my tongue. But I'm still really sorry.
jokes.setup: Monica, pumped from her confrontation, immediately runs after Mrs. Green to apologize again
jokes.punchline: She falls, hurts herself, but continues apologizing through the pain — the physical comedy of her pratfall combined with the commitment to the apology
jokes.explanation: The pratfall as an immediate deflation of Monica's hard-won confidence is a satisfying payoff. 'I bit my tongue. But I'm still really sorry' while lisping is a funny specific detail — the physical injury doesn't stop her compulsive need to apologize. Good physical comedy inference.

jokes.text: Rachel Green, let's play Bamboozled.
jokes.setup: Joey promises to quiz Rachel on baby care knowledge
jokes.punchline: He announces it as 'Bamboozled' — recontextualizing the game show as a baby quiz
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural callback that merges the two episode plots. Joey using Bamboozled to genuinely help Rachel is a sweet and funny convergence. The audience has been primed to love Bamboozled, so the reveal that it's the vehicle for Rachel's quiz earns a warm response.

jokes.text: [MIMICS BABY CRYING] / Uh, check if it's wet, check if it's hungry, burp it.
jokes.setup: Joey gives an 'audio question' — a baby crying sound — as part of Bamboozled.
jokes.punchline: Joey mimicking a baby crying as a formal game show question is inherently absurd. Rachel answers correctly, playing the game completely straight.
jokes.explanation: Joey crying like a baby as a formal game show device applied to real parenting questions is a funny juxtaposition. Rachel's earnest participation makes it sweeter.

jokes.text: Now, do you want another question or a Wicked Wango Card? / A card. A card. I pick a card. / Oh, I'm sorry. You've been Bamboozled. You're gonna be a terrible mother.
jokes.setup: Rachel is doing brilliantly on the baby quiz; Joey offers her a Wicked Wango Card option
jokes.punchline: Rachel excitedly picks the card — which reveals she's 'been Bamboozled' and delivers the punchline 'you're gonna be a terrible mother'
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and a masterclass in structural comedy. The Wicked Wango Card (introduced as a meaningless mechanic in the first Bamboozled scene) becomes the trap Rachel falls into. After successfully answering every real baby care question, her greed for the bonus loses her the game — and the punchline 'you're gonna be a terrible mother' is the game show's penalty. This works on multiple levels: it pays off the Bamboozled running gag, it ties both episode plots together, and 'you're gonna be a terrible mother' is darkly funny as the consequence of picking a card in a baby quiz. The irony that she actually KNOWS the answers but falls for the gimmick is thematically resonant with her journey. High craft, high impact, and the ideal episode closer.

jokes.text: I've lost sight of why we're doing this.
jokes.setup: Rachel has just been told she'll be a terrible mother by a fake game show
jokes.punchline: Rachel's flat 'I've lost sight of why we're doing this' — which is both completely valid and also funny as a confession of absurdist confusion
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the entire episode. Rachel's bewildered admission captures both her emotional state and the audience's amused recognition of the absurdity. 'I've lost sight of why we're doing this' is quietly great — it functions as a tag on the joke, a character moment, and a meta-comment on the whole Bamboozled subplot. Excellent economy.

tmdb_overview: Monica and Phoebe throw Rachel a baby shower but forget to invite Rachel's mom. During the baby shower Rachel panics when she realizes she has no idea how to look after the baby after the birth. Meanwhile, Joey auditions for a job as a host for a new game show called "Bamboozled", and Chandler and Ross help him practice.
insight: Baby shower chaos sustains 2.8 jokes-per-minute through escalating cringe over 24 minutes.
